title: Washing and shrouds
hookLine: the body is washed and dressed in plain white shrouds, the same for everyone
last: KINDNESS TO THE DEAD IS TRUE KINDNESS.

cards: Families were running away from their own dead. That's the scene the Talmud describes.
Burial had become so expensive, with fine clothes and costly display, that for some, the cost of a funeral was harder to bear than the death itself. Some relatives would leave the body and flee.
Then Rabban Gamliel, a leader of his generation, made a request about his own funeral: bury me in plain linen. The people followed him, and carried out their own dead in linen too.

teach.b: Before that plain linen comes tahara, purification: the ritual washing of the body, done by the holy society.
The body is cleaned gently and thoroughly, the face kept covered and only the part being washed uncovered, out of modesty. Then water is poured over the whole body in a continuous flow.
Members say verses and prayers as they work, and in some communities, at the end, they say: tehorah hi, she is pure, or tahor hu, he is pure.

Then the shrouds, called tachrichim: plain white garments, usually linen or cotton, sewn by hand, with no pockets, and in some traditions no buttons or knots. A Yiddish saying goes: shrouds have no pockets.

A rabbi and a cab driver, a philanthropist and a person who died with nothing: dressed alike. That goes back to Rabban Gamliel. Equality in death wasn't an accident; it was a decision, made so no family would be shamed.
Some men are also wrapped in their own tallit, the prayer shawl, with one fringe cut.
In the book of Job, after losing everything, Job says: "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither."
Tahara treats the body almost as a newborn is treated: washed by others, wrapped by others, held by others.

how: Before a traditional Jewish burial, members of the chevra kadisha perform tahara, washing the body with care and pouring water over it, then dress it in simple white shrouds called tachrichim; some men are also wrapped in their tallit.

games.q: you're Rabban Gamliel. funerals are so costly that families flee their dead. what do you do?
o: ask to be buried in plain linen yourself.
pay for every funeral from the treasury.
games.why: he asked for plain linen at his own burial, and the people followed him.

practice: Look at what you're wearing, and notice what in it says something about you: a brand, a ring, a badge, a style. Without judging any of it, ask: if all of this were replaced with one plain white garment, what would still be me?
If you pray, you can say the line from Job slowly, or sit in silence.

wordCard.voice: Tahara. Purification: the washing of the body, the flow of water, and plain white shrouds, the same for everyone. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: purification, the washing before burial.

carryVoice: Your line: everyone equal in death. No family shamed, no one set apart. See you tomorrow.
